subsystems.name: Reactor core and fuel
subsystems.role: holds a self-sustaining fission chain reaction in a small, very light package.
parts: highly enriched uranium metal alloy fuel (the Kilopower approach)
boron carbide control and shutdown rods

subsystems.name: Heat transport
subsystems.role: moves heat from the core to the converters without pumps or moving coolant.
parts: sodium heat pipes bonded into the core

subsystems.name: Heat rejection
subsystems.role: dumps waste heat to space — in vacuum, radiators must be big, and there is two to three times more waste heat than electricity.

subsystems.name: Shielding and siting
subsystems.role: protects crew, equipment and the lander from neutrons and gamma rays.

subsystems.name: Control and autonomy
subsystems.role: runs unattended for years, including through the lunar night.

subsystems.name: Lander interface
subsystems.role: carries a fuelled, subcritical reactor to the surface and sets it down.

buildSteps.title: Make the fuel
buildSteps.detail: Uranium is enriched, alloyed and cast into a monolithic core rather than the fuel rods of a terrestrial reactor.

buildSteps.title: Build in the heat pipes
buildSteps.detail: Sodium-filled heat pipes are bonded into the core so heat leaves by evaporation and condensation, with no pumps.

buildSteps.title: Assemble core and reflector
buildSteps.detail: The core is surrounded by a beryllium reflector, with boron carbide rods that keep it shut down before launch and can stop it afterwards.

buildSteps.title: Build the convertors
buildSteps.detail: Free-piston Stirling engines with linear alternators are assembled and run for thousands of hours to prove lifetime.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the radiators
buildSteps.detail: Lightweight panels with embedded heat pipes are made to fold for launch and unfold on the surface.

buildSteps.title: Test the whole system on the ground
buildSteps.detail: Electric heaters first, then a fuelled critical test in a shielded facility — the approach taken by the 2018 KRUSTY experiment in Nevada, which ran a 1 kW-class reactor.

buildSteps.title: Qualify for launch
buildSteps.detail: Launch safety analysis and containment are prepared; the reactor stays subcritical until it is safely on the surface.

buildSteps.title: Land, deploy and start up
buildSteps.detail: A lander sets the unit down, radiators unfold, it is buried or bermed with regolith for shielding, and the reactor is brought critical autonomously and run through a 14-day lunar night.

prerequisites.why: a handful have flown — SNAP-10A in 1965 and Soviet radar-satellite reactors — but none has operated on a planetary surface, and ground tests such as KRUSTY are the current state of the art.
they must run for a decade without maintenance; terrestrial Stirling machines exist but not at this lifetime and reliability.
rejecting tens of kilowatts in vacuum needs large area that must still fit on a lander.

prerequisites.tech: Nuclear launch approval and fuelled-payload handling
prerequisites.why: the pacing item is qualifying fuelled hardware for launch and landing, not the reactor physics.
commercial lunar landers are flying, but delivering and placing a shielded reactor is a step beyond current demonstrated payloads.

pathway.milestone: a 1 kW-class ground demonstration completed (KRUSTY, 2018); 40 kW-class conceptual designs funded by NASA and the US Department of Energy
pathway.unlocks: confidence that a small fast reactor with heat pipes and Stirling convertors can work.

pathway.milestone: a complete flight-configured unit tested on the ground, including launch qualification
pathway.unlocks: a design that can actually be put on a lander.

pathway.milestone: a reactor demonstrated on the lunar surface and run through the night
pathway.unlocks: proven surface power for habitats and instruments independent of sunlight.

pathway.milestone: multiple units scaled to hundreds of kilowatts or megawatts
pathway.unlocks: outposts, in-situ propellant production and, eventually, power for industry on the Moon and Mars.
